I don’t love the idea of opening my blogging career with a blog centered on a man, much less to a man with the kind of mildly misogynistic, very superiority-complex-ful cult following that Nolan has. Unfortunately, this topic has the lowest activation energy for me to finish, given the fit of passion I wrote most of the notes for it after coming home from the AMC IMAX theater at 1 AM.

To preface where this critique comes from—I’m someone who has consumed and continues to consume ridiculous amounts of media, both good and bad and everywhere in between. I’m also a hobby photographer. Naturally then, when I watch a movie, to me the storytelling and the composition are just as important as the actual story being told. Christopher Nolan being a veteran storyteller with some of the highest praise and controversy on the western film market, I went into my first Nolan movie with some trepidation, some hope.

Nolan in this movie is engaging in age old beloved practice of retelling stories. Specifically myths. Many of us love retellings for many reasons—a small plot twist or a different perspective can completely turn a myth on its head, revealing to us faces of the world storytellers before us may never have conceived of. Moreover, a retelling often reveals to us just as much about the perceiver and the reality they live in rather as it does about the original storyteller. The retelling is a projection of the lens of our reteller. Given the many many iterations a reteller can draw from, what they choose to draw from or choose to discard reveals what they find realistic or useful. What they see existing or want to bring to life. When we watch Nolan’s Odyssey, we are not only watching the original myth, but specifically Nolan’s version of it which wraps the assumptions, anxieties and appetites of the country at large.

First, I must address the filming technique itself. Filming the entire thing on 70 mm IMAX is definitely an admirable undertaking, rightly drawing massive attention. Getting IMAX tickets felt akin to getting concert tickets, except these theaters were running the movie nearly 16 hours a day, 7 days a week, and were still booked out.

The 70 mm was *gorgeous*. Naturally, with 70 mm being in its infancy, the cinematographers do at times struggle to find their voice. At certain points in the movie, when the composition showed signs of thought, the camera work was incredibly striking in 70mm. My favourite scenes shot throughout the show were those on sea and in half darkness, half light. I also absolutely adored the shot framing Odysseus dropping out of the horse and some of his scenes right next to the statue of Athena. However, most of the composition is just a bit hollow (just a tad) and the colour grading just off (just a bit). Occasionally the grading would differ drastically between cuts which, intentionally or not, didn't truly add any true artistic value (that is they did not echo mood shifts, perception changes or otherwise complement storytelling). Both of these faults, to me, can be excusable. Filming for 70mm seems incredibly challenging, and at some point artistic vision has to yield to the camera people’s physical and time limitations.

My only real complaint with the 70mm in *The Odyssey* is the shifting camera focus in indoor close up scenes. I am talking about scenes such as where Penelope and Odysseus are on their bed talking, or when Athena and Odysseus’ faces are blown up in the same shot. The focus shift was a little too jarring for the most part—the blurring and unbarring of people was noticeable and annoying. Moreover, every so often they would spend too much time with the plane of focus in between the people when trying to change focus from one person to another. Obviously it is easy for me to sit on a couch and criticize the camera work. I do not doubt focusing with the equipment in such low light settings that require the blown up aperture was technically really hard. But, I'm of the school of thought that a storyteller must play to her equipment's benefit, especially when forcing your equipment to do something it's clearly not built for distracts your audience (me). I understand that it's all the rage to shift focus between speakers to highlight their faces when they're having intimate conversations, but I genuinely think it was too heavy handed and obvious to be artistically impressive. A truly masterful director would do it deftly enough that I wouldn't notice the process until I went hunting.

Despite this complaint, the camerawork remains a highlight for me. I hope that Nolan’s commercial success in IMAX theaters and the *Odyssey*’s visuals both good and bad inspire cinematographers to greater and greater experimentation with 70mm. I can't wait to see the unexplored terrain yet to come in IMAX cinema.

In terms of the story and writing itself, the last fifteen minutes saved the entire experience for me. Nolan’s motivation really comes into focus with a very timely message at the end, and I see his vision. I can imagine the rush that must have gone through him when inspiration struck him. Do I think he needed 3 hours to get to the point? Perhaps not. The middle did drag for me, but the nugget of creativity that inspires and defines the retelling was definitely phenomenal. Further thoughts on the ending, I will isolate at the end of this review to avoid spoilers for anyone who may stumble across this review without having watched the movie.

Yet, however much I liked the concept, the execution and the details of the story itself, I had many a bone to pick.

First, we talk about women.

Nolan’s women were thin as air, even if they were painted vaguely righteous colours. My sister texted me telling me how she loved “when Anne Hathaway got mad at telemachus and said ‘I am the queen ive ruled this city for 20 years’”. I actually hated it. Why?

How long did Penelope take to utter this thought? What actions lead up to her claim? What does this half bitten out sentence half buried in weakness and helplessness?

Nolan understands on a logical level that this is the feminist line, the correct thought to highlight. But does he truly understand, emotionally, how it manifests?

Where do we see Penelope actually governing in the movie? Where does she have any authority that doesn't look like a tantrum? We get multiple jump scare scenes (how many do we really need to drive home Odysseus’ PTSD and the propagation of hostility towards strangers?), but none showing Penlope doing any paper work behind the screen as she weaves. Even at the very end, the calling off the feast when Odysseus is getting beat up, that is done by telemachus. The internet seems obsessed with the exclusion of Penelope’s pick up the bed challenge for her suitors. With an already long (by American standards) runtime, logically Nolan can only really show so much. He actually picks a task that somewhat echoes the bare bones and beats of the bed task. Penelope sets a task she *knows* only Odysseus can succeed at. The way \[dick guy\]’s face drops when she reveals the task, anyone who knew the task would realise immediately that she chose an impossible task for anyone other than Odysseus. However, there is an interesting difference in the two tasks that is a bit telling about what constitutes a Hero and a Man in the American subconscious. The bed task, Odysseus could only pass due to *his knowledge*, further a knowledge that he *physically* *could not* complete the task. The bow task, only Odysseus can pass because only he is *physically strong* enough. The task requires no smarts from Odysseus, and no humility about the extent of his physical ability or his ability to challenge nature and win. In America, physical invincibility makes the hero. Might makes right.

The choice of task itself, truly does not matter much. The internet, as always, has indexed on the superficial, while ignoring the crux of the problem. The main issue with the chosen task, I feel, remains the directing of Penelope’s passivity. What rankled me was the dissonance between the bare bones plot and the actual visual story. We are told she’s smart—she chose a good task. We are told she’s brave—she says she held the country together. However, visually you have Penelope stuck in a room with a huge number of men with no way to defend herself (except, of course Odysseus). Beyond setting the task, Penelope does nothing active during the scene, until the ending when she pushes another woman down into the violence and flee. She also has no visual shots giving her power (for e.g. standing on a podium, framing that puts her above anyone, any sort of visual shot with her holding strength). Does that not rankle you? The depiction of a woman as anything but a passive vessel for men’s violence and avarice and sins, is having expectations beyond this the default too feminist of me? Am I asking every single piece of media to #be feminist and #send a message, or am I simply asking for men to deign to show women in stories *as they would have been*? Why do I have to suffer such *lazy* writing, just because men cannot look beyond their distorted understanding of women, and the difference possession or absence of a goddamn penis makes to a person?

And let's talk about that screen between Penelope and her suitors. The moment I saw it, a chord of dissonance struck within me. I went back to check and I was correct—the screen is visual grammar popularly associated with Islamic tradition, invoking a sort of seeing without seeing between people of different genders. Ancient Greece did not have such screens. To clarify, I do not accuse Nolan to do this on purpose. However, he shares the same group consciousness as the rest of us Americans and in the American subconscious, Islam is associated with sexist oppression. He borrows this visual grammar, to paint an increasingly harrowing environment for Penelope. By having her sit behind a screen, doing nothing but mourning, saying nothing to defend herself or take control, not being able to turn out the rowdy men in her own house—Nolan has painted an entirely more helpless portrait of Penelope than say if she had her own quarters where she can exist beyond the men who want her hand or if she was openly present in the hall. Again, despite whatever the characters say, visually we are told only one thing about Penelope—that she is weak, helpless and has nothing to do other than be harassed by her suitors until her husband comes back from war.

Beyond Penelope too, no woman is really fleshed out more than the vague notion of a plot vehicle. In fact, most of Nolan’s characters beyond Odysseus are not. It just so happens that the few who are—Telemachus, the shepherd, the antagonist guy, Elliott page’s character—are all men. Most of Odysseus’ men on the boat, I have no memories of them truly. The only woman in the entire film I can stand remains Helen of Troy. Even though she too remains mostly a plot vehicle to depict the moral ambiguity of the Greeks, she carried within her a life that was not explained to us. (Where did she get the scar from? What does she think? Who is she?) I think the mystery ironically makes her a better fleshed out character than any other woman in the movie, simply because Nolan is letting her live and breathe without trying all of her motivations back to the men or the protagonist. Moreover, casting Lupita Nyong'o as Helen is a brilliant move by Nolan. She’s breathtakingly eye-catching and embodies the mystery of Helen of Troy perfectly. (Please, I too would go to war for her). I am glad the crew stood firm in her casting despite the discourse it has sparked in Hollywood.

I can continue dissecting the women in *The Odyssey*, but the rest of my takes and thoughts, I trust the internet to avail the populace of, without any intervention from me. Beyond women, I mostly concern myself with the big ticket theme and its delivery in *The Odyssey*. If you have not watched the movie yet, I would recommend pausing and coming back once you have seen it.

To reiterate, I appreciate Nolan’s vision with the movie and theme. His spin focusing “breaking the law of Zeus” adds a layer of meaning and a new powerful and creative perspective to an old myth by highlighting breaking basic human regard and decency we owe others leads only to downfall and ruin, even if it is to bring victories to the nation. In a time where a lot of the U.S. is reckoning with after-effects from five decades of meddling in affairs abroad in ways that would definitely be considered breaking basic human decency (insert examples from the middle east), the movie rings a timely reminder.

However, I do think the execution and delivery of this message could have been tightened up immensely. I overheard a fellow watcher say that Nolan has a way of making 3 hours feel like nothing. As someone raised on routine 3 hour long musicals from Bollywood, I would say there are 3 hour movies I like that go faster. I did have to clock out in the middle because I was a little bored, I'm not going lie\! The fighting was a bit much for me--it felt like a jump scare horror movie in the middle which I was not a fan of. The soundtrack was also *so loud* at times that I could not even process what was happening. I loved loved *loved* the three chimes of athena’s helmet falling that repeated as a motif every time Zeus’ law breaks or Odysseus runs into a cold deadly welcome. However the overly loud soundtrack and dragged out fight scenes diluted the effect a bunch for me. Also, while it was a nice surprise for the last fifteen minutes to tie everything together and tell me the theme + what I was hearing with the three strikes, (frankly saving the movie for me), it isolates the actual effect and time of thinking to the end fifteen minutes of the movie. I personally think this movie could have easily been thirty minutes shorter and started tying everything together a tad quicker. Also, while a cool concept, I had truly started rolling my eyes a bit at every invocation of Zeus' law throughout... it started feeling a little annoying and trite the fiftieth time.

I say all of these things, knowing full well that it is Christopher Nolan’s name that sells out movies at box offices, not mine. Clearly, he understands how to make movies that Hollywood and the American populace want more than I ever could\! Quoting 2 AM post *Odyssey* Shruti, “what I'm realising from this exercise \[in reviewing\] is that people are dumb as rocks.” If they were more used to critically watching media, the way that he handholds and spoon feeds you really would have rankled more people. Makes me wonder, if we really do need to do something for media literacy in America… Reading between the lines only makes movies more fun, I promise\! (I also have a theory that Nolan’s movie really appeals to people who like to feel smart because they can connect the thoughts and talk about the themes afterwards because he makes it so obvious without having to engage emotionally or even interpretively very much with the movie… as chat rephrased for me- Nolan gives his audience the pleasure of “discovering a theme” without requiring them to wrestle with ambiguity, contradiction, or emotional complexity themselves by telling them exactly what to think.)

The last note I have from my 2 AM brain dump is - “I also may have a bone to pick about racial divides but not as sure about that.” However, I am too lazy to further ponder upon the vague notions I had about the screentime and role of any non-white actors/characters despite their inclusion. I would love to hear any thoughts you may have about it though\!

Cheers,  
Shruti
